changes.new: При нескольких ускорителях можно обменяться эмбеддингами и собрать общую матрицу. Нужно согласовать индексы положительных пар и передачу градиента через обмен. ### GradCache: full-batch negatives with chunked encoder passes With two training pairs, let both the query and document inputs be the rows of the identity matrix. A shared linear encoder starts with an identity weight matrix, so the score matrix is also the identity. Each query has one positive with score 1 and one negative with score 0. At temperature 1, the positive probability is about 0.7311 and the mean loss is about 0.3133. Splitting the two pairs into singleton losses removes both negatives: each softmax then has one entry and both losses are zero. GradCache keeps the two-by-two loss. It changes when the encoder's computation graphs are built and discarded. First, encode both queries and both documents without recording encoder activations. These four vectors are enough to calculate the contrastive loss and its derivatives with respect to the vectors. Then recompute each encoder chunk with autograd enabled and propagate its already calculated representation gradient into the encoder weights. The published paper describes the sequence as follows. The excerpt retains the original English; the numeric example and executable check below are Bookvar additions. > **Step1: Graph-less Forward** Before gradient computation, we first run an extra > encoder forward pass for each batch instance to get its representation. > Importantly, this forward pass runs without constructing the computation > graph. We collect and store all representations computed. > > **Step2: Representation Gradient Computation and Caching** We then compute the > contrastive loss for the batch based on the representation from Step1 and > have a corresponding computation graph constructed. Despite the mathematical > derivation, automatic differentiation system is used in actual implementation, > which automatically supports variations of contrastive loss. A backward pass > is then run to populate gradients for each representation. Note that the > encoder is not included in this gradient computation. > > **Step3: Sub-batch Gradient Accumulation** We run encoder forward one sub-batch > at a time to compute representations and build the corresponding computation > graph. We take the sub-batch’s representation gradients from the cache and > run back propagation through the encoder. Gradients are accumulated for > encoder parameters across all sub-batches. > > **Step4: Optimization** When all sub-batches are processed, we can step the > optimizer to update model parameters as if the full batch is processed in a > single forward-backward pass. *Luyu Gao, Yunyi Zhang, Jiawei Han and Jamie Callan, [Scaling Deep Contrastive Learning Batch Size under Memory Limited Setup, §3.3](https://aclanthology.org/2021.repl4nlp-1.31/). CC BY 4.0 under the [ACL Anthology policy](https://aclanthology.org/faq/copyright/). Selected prose paragraphs reproduced verbatim; the intervening equations and the sentence defining the cache symbols are omitted.* For the two-pair example, the derivative with respect to the first query vector is approximately $(-0.13447,0.13447)$. The first document gets the same derivative; the second query and document get $(0.13447,-0.13447)$. Each derivative includes the factor $1/2$ from the mean over the two queries. A cached derivative therefore already includes the full-batch reduction. Dividing it by the number of chunks again would make the parameter gradient too small. Let $h_i=f_\theta(x_i)$ be a representation and $g_i=\partial L/\partial h_i$ its cached gradient. The chain rule gives $$ \begin{aligned} \nabla_\theta L&=\sum_i J_i^\top g_i,\\ J_i&=\frac{\partial f_\theta(x_i)}{\partial\theta}. \end{aligned} $$ Recomputing one chunk supplies its vector–Jacobian product without keeping all other encoder graphs alive. In code, the scalar surrogate $\sum_i h_i^\top\operatorname{stopgrad}(g_i)$ has the required parameter gradient. Its numeric value is not the original loss, so it is not a replacement for the loss in training logs. With shared encoder weights, query-side and document-side contributions accumulate into the same parameter tensors. The CPU check below uses a linear encoder, not a pretrained language model. It compares every weight derivative with an ordinary full-batch backward pass. No optimizer update happens between chunks. ```python import torch from torch import nn from torch.nn import functional as F def cached_encoder_grad(model, queries, documents, chunk_size): model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) with torch.no_grad(): q = torch.cat([model(x) for x in queries.split(chunk_size)]) d = torch.cat([model(x) for x in documents.split(chunk_size)]) q = q.detach().requires_grad_() d = d.detach().requires_grad_() labels = torch.arange(len(queries), device=queries.device) loss = F.cross_entropy(q @ d.T, labels) dq, dd = torch.autograd.grad(loss, (q, d)) for inputs, gradients in [(queries, dq), (documents, dd)]: for x, g in zip(inputs.split(chunk_size), gradients.split(chunk_size)): # g already contains the mean reduction over all queries. (model(x) * g).sum().backward() return loss.detach(), [p.grad.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()] inputs = torch.eye(2, dtype=torch.float64) encoder = nn.Linear(2, 2, bias=False, dtype=torch.float64) with torch.no_grad(): encoder.weight.copy_(torch.eye(2, dtype=torch.float64)) full_loss = F.cross_entropy(encoder(inputs) @ encoder(inputs).T, torch.arange(2)) full_loss.backward() full_gradient = encoder.weight.grad.detach().clone() cached_loss, cached_gradients = cached_encoder_grad(encoder, inputs, inputs, 1) assert torch.allclose(cached_loss, full_loss.detach()) assert torch.allclose(cached_gradients[0], full_gradient, atol=1e-12) print(round(float(cached_loss), 6)) # 0.313262 print(full_gradient) # tensor([[-0.2689, 0.2689], # [ 0.2689, -0.2689]], dtype=torch.float64) encoder.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) for x in inputs.split(1): singleton_loss = F.cross_entropy(encoder(x) @ encoder(x).T, torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.long)) singleton_loss.backward() assert torch.count_nonzero(encoder.weight.grad) == 0 ``` This implementation assumes deterministic, example-independent encoder computations. A training-mode Transformer usually has dropout. Its recomputed chunk must use the same random choices as its first pass, including the separate query and document passes when weights are shared. Otherwise the cached $g_i$ belongs to one sampled representation but multiplies the Jacobian of another. The [authors’ implementation](https://github.com/luyug/GradCache/blob/906f03835fbc183132a9db32612a9e8f180ca3b4/src/grad_cache/grad_cache.py) records a [RandContext](https://github.com/luyug/GradCache/blob/906f03835fbc183132a9db32612a9e8f180ca3b4/src/grad_cache/context_managers.py) for each chunk and restores CPU and relevant CUDA generator states for its recomputation. The short example does not implement that mechanism and must not be used unchanged with stochastic encoders. Restoring RNG state does not restore arbitrary mutable model state. Training-mode BatchNorm, for example, computes statistics from the chunk; changing the chunk changes the function, and repeated forwards can update running statistics twice. Equality to a full-batch gradient requires matching the actual forward function, its parameters, stochastic choices and state. Floating-point accumulation can also change the final low-order bits. For a fixed encoder chunk size, retained encoder activations no longer grow with the full contrastive batch. The representation and gradient caches still grow as $O(Bd)$; the explicit score matrix in this example grows as $O(B^2)$. Its loss computation can itself become the memory bottleneck. An extra encoder forward pass also costs time. The paper's runtime measurements describe its DPR experiment, not a fixed overhead for every model and GPU.
